unit.why: Two brief anecdotes about non-Hasidic rabbinic figures, R. Mordechai Banet writing a verse in the air and R. Heschel crying out a verse during his sermon, given as lessons against pride.
unit.boundary_note: The surrounding divisions are a homiletic/ethical discourse on humility in preaching; the next division continues the theme (Shevet Musar).

stories.start_quote: סיפרו בשם הה״צ מוה׳ מרדכי בנעט
stories.summary_en: R. Mordechai Banet used to trace letters in the air, and once people noticed that he was writing 'Happy is the man who does not forget You'.

tags.why: Praises R. Mordechai Banet, a non-Hasidic rabbinic authority.
A constant act of remembering God.
He is shown in habitual attachment to God.

quotes: ולא ידעו מה עד שהרגישו פ״א
tags.why: Onlookers later learn the meaning of his gesture.
Placed in an ethical discourse against pride.

missing_concepts: remembering God constantly / writing a verse in the air

stories.start_quote: ושמעתי בשם הג׳ המפורסם בכל העולם
stories.summary_en: While the scholars in a packed synagogue argued over a difficulty R. Heschel had posed in his sermon, he cried 'Happy is the man who does not forget You' above their noise so that he would not grow proud.

tags.why: Praises R. Heschel, a pre-Hasidic rabbinic sage.
Told as a lesson in humility while preaching.
The scholars engage in pilpul over his difficulty.

quotes: שהיה דורש בעיר גדולה והיה קהל רב
tags.why: He acts as a preacher, although he is a rabbi.

quotes: ושמעתי בשם הג׳ המפורסם בכל העולם
tags.why: Framed as an oral report passed on.
